title: I built a virtual stock community where AI agents trade, debate, and compete on their own
summary:
Hey everyone!

I've been working on a side project called AgorUno (Agora + Uno). It's a virtual community where AI agents autonomously discuss stocks, make paper trades, and interact with each other.

Each agent has its own portfolio, trading history, and performance record. You can explore their activities through a 3D world, see which stocks they're interested in, follow their discussions, and check the AI League rankings.

There's also a prediction system where agents compete using virtual points. No real money is traded, and visitors can only observe. I attached a short GIF of the main screen. I'm curious what you think.

Would you find something like this interesting to follow? What would you improve or add? It's still an experiment, so honest feedback would be really helpful!

[Web: agoruno.vercel.app]

title: MCP's file transfer draft keeps bytes out of your model's context: 5 mechanics and 3 open security questions
summary:
Yesterday the MCP maintainers published the first draft of an extension for moving files between clients and tools. If you build MCP servers, this is the piece you have been hand-rolling: base64 blobs in tool arguments, bespoke presigned-URL conventions, CSVs pasted into prompts. The extension, identified as io.modelcontextprotocol/files, wants to standardize all of it. It works with protocol revision 2026-07-28 and later, and the maintainers expect it stable before the end of the year.

I read the full announcement and the draft's mechanics. Here is what actually changes for a server author, and where the design still has open holes.

The core design decision: bytes never enter JSON-RPC

title: Before Your AI Agent Spends Money, Ask How Its Approvals Expire
summary:
Most businesses that let an AI agent touch money do the sensible thing: they put a person in the loop. The agent drafts a refund, a purchase order, or a credit, and a manager approves it before anything happens. That approval step is the main reason owners feel safe letting an agent near the checkbook.

But an approval is only as good as its timing. Picture this: a customer asks for a $500 refund. The agent prepares it and sends the request to a manager. The manager is out, so a colleague handles the customer by phone and refunds them directly. Two days later the manager catches up on approvals and clicks yes. Does the agent now send a second $500?

title: Transferring 300,000 small ArrayBuffers from a Worker was slower than copying them (in Chromium)
summary:
I run a DXF viewer that works entirely in the browser. DXF is the text format CAD programs use to exchange drawings. A Web Worker reads the file and builds the drawing (a collection of typed arrays of coordinates), hands it to the page with postMessage, and the page draws it on a canvas.

A Worker's postMessage can transfer an ArrayBuffer instead of copying it: buffers listed in the second argument are handed to the other side without a copy, and become unusable on the sending side. It is the standard advice for passing large data to and from a Worker, and when I added the DXF viewer, I made the Worker move every typed array in its result that way.

Then a drawing with 100,000 layers took almost 14 seconds to open in Chromium. The time was not spent building the drawing. It was spent handing the result to the page. This post is about that.

title: Less is better: why we removed the AI gateway, MCP and the web UI
summary:
The most secure line of code is the one that is not there.

On the road to 1.0, we did something that rarely makes a changelog look exciting: we deleted features. The AI gateway is gone. The MCP server is gone. The web UI is gone. Together that is roughly 27,000 lines of Rust, TypeScript, tests and documentation that no longer ship with Barbacane.

This post explains why. The short version: we are building a light, robust, zero-trust API gateway, and every one of those features was pulling in the opposite direction.

What we took out

The AI gateway. An ai-proxy dispatcher that spoke to OpenAI, Anthropic and Ollama behind one OpenAI-compatible surface (Chat Completions, the Responses API, an aggregated model catalog), plus four middlewares for prompt guarding, token limits, cost tracking and response redaction. title: Gemini Decisions API
summary:
Gemini Decisions API

Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question.

It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million.

Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.
